intro: Every society has ideas about who does what work, who gives orders and who must bow. In this unit you will visit India, China, Japan and Korea. In each place, people were sorted into groups by birth, by learning or by the sword. Those groups shaped where people lived, whom they married and how they spoke to one another.

You will also meet people who questioned these orders. A Dalit boy who sat on a sack at school grew up to help write India's Constitution. Poets sang that God looks at the heart, not at birth. Japanese reformers, many of them samurai, ended their own class. Korean scholars made an alphabet so ordinary people could read.

By the end, you will be able to explain how varna and jati differ, how exams and birth decided rank in East Asia, and how laws and movements changed these systems. You will weigh different views fairly and back up your ideas with facts from the unit.
bigQuestion: How did Asian societies rank people, and how did people inside those systems work to change them?

title: Social Order in Asia

chapters.title: India: Varna, Jati and Change
chapters.bigQuestion: How did a system of birth groups shape life in India, and how have people worked to change it?

story.title: The Boy on the Sack
story.kicker: A schoolboy was made to sit apart from his classmates, and he grew up to help write the rules for a whole nation.
paragraphs: In the 1890s a small boy named Bhimrao walked to school in the town of Satara, in western India. He carried a folded piece of sacking under his arm. His family belonged to the Mahar community. Many people at the time treated Mahars as untouchable, which meant others would not share food, water or even a floor mat with them.

At school Bhimrao spread his sack in a corner and sat on it, away from the other children. Some teachers would not touch his notebooks. When he was thirsty, he could not turn on the water tap himself. He had to wait for a school worker to pour water into his cupped hands from above. If no worker came, he went without.

Bhimrao was a hungry reader, and his father pushed him to study. He finished high school at a time when very few Mahar children did. Then he won scholarships to study abroad. He earned advanced degrees from Columbia University in New York and from the London School of Economics. People came to know him as Dr. B. R. Ambedkar.

Ambedkar spent his life fighting the rules that had shut him out. When India became independent in 1947, he was asked to chair the committee that drafted its new Constitution. That Constitution, in force from 1950, says that untouchability is abolished. The boy who once sat on a sack helped write the highest law of a nation of hundreds of millions.
story.think: What do you think it felt like for Ambedkar to write a law against the treatment he lived through as a child? Why might his own experience have mattered?

lessons.title: Four Groups in Old Texts
lessons.mainIdea: Ancient Hindu texts described society as four broad groups called varnas.
reading: More than 3,000 years ago, poets in northern India composed hymns in the Sanskrit language. These hymns were collected in the Rig Veda, one of the oldest religious texts in the world. One hymn pictures society as the body of a great cosmic being. Different groups of people come from different parts of that body.

Later texts built on this picture. They named four *varnas*, or broad groups. Brahmins were priests and teachers. Kshatriyas were rulers and warriors. Vaishyas were traders and farmers. Shudras were laborers who served the other three. Each group was given its own duties, called *dharma*.

It helps to remember that varna was mostly an ideal written down by priests and scholars. It was a way of saying how society should be ordered. Real life was far messier. Kings sometimes came from families outside the warrior varna, and many people did work that did not match the old list.

words.d: one of four broad social groups described in ancient Hindu texts
in Hindu thought, a person's duty or right way of living
a collection of very old Sanskrit hymns, among the oldest religious texts in the world

look.title: A Society Pictured as a Body
look.text: Imagine a drawing of a giant human body. Priests come from the mouth. Warriors come from the arms. Traders and farmers come from the thighs. Laborers come from the feet. The drawing says every part is needed for the body to live. It also places the parts from top to bottom.
look.prompt: What two messages could a reader take from this picture? One is about working together. What is the other one about?

check.q: How many varnas did the ancient texts describe?
check.why: The texts named four varnas: Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and Shudras.

check.q: Which varna was linked with priests and teachers?
check.why: Brahmins were the priests and teachers in the varna picture.

check.q: Why does the lesson call varna mostly an ideal?
choices: It was invented by British rulers
It described how society should be, and real life was messier
check.why: Varna was a plan written by priests and scholars; real jobs and rulers often did not match it.

lessons.title: Jati: Thousands of Birth Groups
lessons.mainIdea: In daily life, people belonged to a jati, a local birth group tied to work and marriage.
reading: Picture a village in India 200 years ago. One family makes clay pots. Another weaves cloth. Another washes clothes, and another works leather. Each family belongs to a group that has done this work for generations. Children are born into the group, and they usually marry inside it.

These birth groups are called *jatis*. The word comes from a root meaning birth. India had thousands of jatis, and they differed from region to region. A jati was often linked to a job, and it set rules about marriage, food and who could eat with whom. Some people ranked jatis as higher or lower in *purity*.

The Portuguese, who came to India around 1500, used their word casta, meaning breed or lineage. That word became caste in English. So when people say caste, they often mean jati. Varna was the broad four-part idea in the texts. Jati was the group a person actually lived in every day.

words.d: a local birth group, often tied to a kind of work and to marriage inside the group
an English word, from Portuguese casta, for birth groups such as jatis
an idea that some groups or acts are cleaner in a religious sense than others

look.title: Varna and Jati Side by Side
look.text: Varna: four groups, named in old religious texts, the same list all over India. Jati: thousands of groups, found in real villages and towns, different in each region, tied to a family's work and to who you may marry.
look.prompt: If you visited one village, which would you see more clearly, varna or jati? Explain why.

check.q: What does the word jati come from?
check.why: Jati comes from a root meaning birth, because people were born into their jati.

check.q: Where did the English word caste come from?
check.why: The Portuguese used casta, meaning breed or lineage, and it became caste in English.

check.q: How was jati different from varna?
choices: Jati was a local birth group people lived in every day
Jati appeared only in the Rig Veda
check.why: Varna was a broad four-part idea in texts; jatis were thousands of real local groups.

lessons.title: Outside the Four Groups
lessons.mainIdea: Some communities were pushed below the four varnas and treated as untouchable.
reading: Some jobs were seen as polluting. These included sweeping streets, removing dead animals, tanning leather and handling the dead at cremation grounds. The communities who did this work were often placed outside the four varnas altogether. Other people treated them as *untouchable*.

Being treated as untouchable meant daily rules of separation. In many places these communities could not draw water from the village well. They could not enter many temples. Some had to live at the edge of the village. These rules were enforced by custom and by pressure from powerful groups, and they varied by region.

Today many people from these communities call themselves *Dalit*. The word means broken or crushed in Marathi and Sanskrit. Leaders chose it with pride, to name the harm done to them and their shared strength. The Indian government uses the term Scheduled Castes for these communities in its laws.

words.d: an old label for groups whom others refused to touch or share with; now rejected and outlawed
a name many people once called untouchable chose for themselves; it means broken or crushed
the legal term the Indian government uses for Dalit communities

look.title: A Well in the Village
look.text: A village has one deep well with clean, cool water. For generations, one community has been told it may not use it. Its families walk a long way to a muddy stream instead. No written law says this. Everyone simply knows the rule, and breaking it brings punishment from neighbors.
look.prompt: How can a rule be powerful even if it is never written down? What would it take to change it?

check.q: Which kind of work was often seen as polluting?
check.why: Work such as tanning leather and removing dead animals was often labeled polluting.

check.q: What does the word Dalit mean?
check.why: Dalit means broken or crushed; leaders chose it to name the harm and their shared strength.

check.q: What term does the Indian government use in law for Dalit communities?
check.why: Indian laws use Scheduled Castes for these communities.

lessons.title: Voices Inside Hinduism
lessons.mainIdea: Many Hindu poets, saints and reformers taught that devotion to God matters more than birth.
reading: In the 1400s a poet named Ravidas lived in the city of Varanasi. He came from a leather-working community that others looked down on. Yet he sang songs of love for God that people still sing today. His message was simple: God is found by a loving heart, not by a high birth.

Ravidas was part of the *bhakti* movement. Bhakti means loving devotion. Across many centuries, bhakti saints wrote in everyday languages instead of Sanskrit. Many of them, including women and people from low-ranked jatis, taught that anyone could reach God. Their songs spread through villages and gave people dignity.

Hindu reformers kept this work going in modern times. In the 1800s and 1900s, groups such as the Arya Samaj argued against untouchability. Mohandas Gandhi called it a sin and campaigned to open temples to all. Hinduism is a very large and varied faith, and its followers have long debated caste among themselves.

words.d: loving devotion to God; a movement of saints and poets who taught that anyone could reach God
a person who works to change and improve a system from the inside

look.title: A Song About the Heart
look.text: The poet says that God does not ask what family you were born into. God looks at the love in your heart. A leather worker who loves God is closer to God than a proud person of high birth.
look.cite: Ravidas, devotional songs, c. 1400s (summary of a common theme)
look.prompt: How does this song challenge the idea that birth decides a person's worth?

check.q: What does bhakti mean?
check.why: Bhakti means loving devotion to God.

check.q: What community did Ravidas come from?
check.why: Ravidas came from a leather-working community that others looked down on.

check.q: Which statement best fits the lesson?
choices: All Hindus have always agreed about caste
Hindus have long debated caste, and many worked against untouchability
check.why: The lesson shows bhakti saints and modern reformers inside Hinduism challenging caste.

lessons.title: Sikh, Muslim and Christian Responses
lessons.mainIdea: Sikhism, Islam and Christianity taught equality before God, though caste habits often lingered.
reading: In the 1500s Guru Nanak founded the Sikh faith in the Punjab region. He taught that all people are equal before one God. Sikhs set up the *langar*, a free community kitchen. Everyone sits on the floor together in rows and eats the same food, whatever their birth. Sikh temples still serve langar today.

Islam came to India through traders and rulers over many centuries. Islam teaches that all believers are equal before God, and people pray side by side in the mosque. Christianity also teaches equality before God. Over time, many people from low-ranked jatis became Muslims or Christians, partly hoping for more respect.

Yet customs are hard to change. Historians find that caste-like divisions often survived inside these communities too. Some families still married only within their old group. Some churches once had separate seating. So the teachings of these faiths opened a path, and their members have kept working to live up to them.

words.d: the free community kitchen at a Sikh temple, where everyone eats together
the idea that people have the same worth and deserve the same treatment

look.title: Sitting in Rows
look.text: Hundreds of people sit on long mats at a Sikh temple. A farmer sits next to a doctor. A child sits next to a stranger. Volunteers walk down the rows with pots of lentils and stacks of flatbread. Everyone gets the same food, served the same way.
look.prompt: What lesson about equality does the langar teach without using any words?

check.q: Who founded the Sikh faith?
check.why: Guru Nanak founded the Sikh faith in the Punjab in the 1500s.

check.q: What happens at a langar?
choices: Everyone eats together, whatever their birth
check.why: At the langar everyone sits together and eats the same free food.

check.q: What do historians find about caste in Muslim and Christian communities in India?
check.why: Customs are hard to change, so caste-like divisions often lingered inside these communities.

lessons.title: The Buddha and Later Buddhists
lessons.mainIdea: The Buddha taught that actions, not birth, make a person worthy, and Ambedkar later turned to Buddhism.
reading: About 2,500 years ago, Siddhartha Gautama lived in northern India. He became known as the Buddha, which means awakened one. He welcomed people of every varna into his community of monks and nuns. He taught that a person becomes noble by good actions, not by birth.

Buddhism spread across Asia but became small in India itself over the centuries. Then, in 1956, B. R. Ambedkar held a large public ceremony in the city of Nagpur. He and a very large crowd of his followers, many of them Dalits, became Buddhists together. Ambedkar said he wanted a faith built on equality and reason.

Ambedkar's step is sometimes called a *conversion*, a change from one religion to another. It was also a political act. It showed that Dalits could choose their own path. Many Indian Buddhists today trace their faith to that day in Nagpur, just weeks before Ambedkar died.

words.d: a title meaning awakened one, given to Siddhartha Gautama, who founded Buddhism
a change from one religion to another

look.title: Noble by Actions
look.text: A person is not a Brahmin by birth, nor an outcast by birth. By actions one becomes an outcast, and by actions one becomes a Brahmin.
look.cite: Sutta Nipata, early Buddhist verses (common English rendering, Vasala Sutta)
look.prompt: What does the Buddha say decides a person's worth? How is that different from the jati system?

check.q: What does the title Buddha mean?
check.why: Buddha means awakened one.

check.q: What did Ambedkar do in Nagpur in 1956?
choices: He and many followers became Buddhists
check.why: In 1956 Ambedkar and a large crowd of followers became Buddhists in Nagpur.

check.q: According to the Buddha, what makes a person noble?
check.why: The Buddha taught that a person becomes noble by actions, not by birth.

lessons.title: Ambedkar's Struggle
lessons.mainIdea: Ambedkar led Dalits in peaceful protests to claim rights such as water and temple entry.
reading: In 1927, in the town of Mahad, there was a public water tank. By law it was open to all. By custom, Dalits were kept away. Ambedkar led thousands of people to the tank, and they drank from it together. This protest is called the Mahad *Satyagraha*, a word meaning holding firmly to truth.

Some upper-caste residents answered with violence, and the struggle went to court. Ambedkar kept organizing. He started newspapers, founded schools and hostels, and formed political groups. He told his followers to get an education, to organize and to demand their rights.

Ambedkar and Gandhi both opposed untouchability, but they disagreed on how to end it. In 1932 they argued over separate elections for Dalits. Gandhi feared this would split Hindus. They reached a deal called the *Poona Pact*, which reserved seats for Dalits instead. Historians still debate which approach did more good.

words.d: Gandhi's word for nonviolent protest; it means holding firmly to truth
a 1932 agreement between Ambedkar and Gandhi that reserved seats in elections for Dalits
a public action that shows people want something changed

look.title: Three Steps
look.text: Ambedkar urged his followers to get educated, to stir people to act, and to organize together so their voices would be heard.
look.cite: B. R. Ambedkar, speeches, 1940s (widely quoted as 'Educate, agitate, organize')
look.prompt: Why might Ambedkar have put education first in his list?

check.q: What happened at the Mahad tank in 1927?
choices: Dalits drank from a public tank they had been kept from
check.why: Ambedkar led thousands of Dalits to drink from the public tank at Mahad.

check.q: What was the Poona Pact?
choices: A 1932 deal that reserved election seats for Dalits
check.why: The Poona Pact of 1932 reserved seats for Dalits instead of separate elections.

check.q: How did Ambedkar and Gandhi relate on untouchability?
choices: Both opposed it but disagreed on how to end it
check.why: Both opposed untouchability, but they disagreed about methods such as separate elections.

lessons.title: Writing the Constitution
lessons.mainIdea: India's Constitution of 1950, drafted under Ambedkar's lead, abolished untouchability.
reading: India won independence from Britain in 1947. The new country needed a *constitution*, a set of highest laws that says how the government works and what rights people have. An assembly of elected members debated it for almost three years. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee, which wrote and revised the text.

The Constitution came into force on January 26, 1950. Indians celebrate that day as Republic Day. It promises every citizen equality before the law. It forbids unfair treatment because of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth. Article 17 says that untouchability is abolished and that practicing it in any form is forbidden.

To *abolish* something is to end it by law. Ambedkar knew a law alone could not change every heart overnight. Still, it changed the rules. Now a Dalit who was turned away from a well or a shop could go to the police and the courts. The state was on the side of equality.

words.d: a country's highest set of laws, describing the government and people's rights
to end something officially by law
January 26, the day India celebrates its Constitution coming into force in 1950

look.title: Article 17
look.text: Untouchability is abolished, and practicing it in any form is forbidden. Enforcing any disadvantage that comes from untouchability is a crime punishable by law.
look.prompt: This article has two parts. What does the first part do? What does the second part add?

check.q: What role did Ambedkar play in writing India's Constitution?
choices: He wrote only the preamble's title
check.why: Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee that wrote and revised the text.

check.q: When did India's Constitution come into force?
check.why: It came into force on January 26, 1950, now celebrated as Republic Day.

check.q: What does Article 17 do?
check.why: Article 17 abolishes untouchability and makes practicing it a crime.

lessons.title: Reservations in Schools and Jobs
lessons.mainIdea: India reserves a share of college seats, government jobs and elected seats for groups held back by caste.
reading: Imagine two students who both want to become engineers. One comes from a family of teachers with books at home. The other is the first in her family to finish school, from a community long kept out of classrooms. India's Constitution asked: how do we give the second student a fair chance?

One answer is *reservations*. A share of seats in public colleges, government jobs and elected bodies is set aside for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. Scheduled Tribes are Indigenous communities, often called Adivasis. In the 1990s reservations were also extended to many groups called Other Backward Classes.

Supporters say reservations have helped millions of families enter colleges, offices and parliament for the first time. Critics say seats should go by merit or by family income, not by group, and that the better-off in each group gain most. Courts have set limits, and the debate continues.

words.d: in India, a share of seats in schools, jobs and legislatures set aside for groups held back by caste
the legal term in India for Indigenous communities, also called Adivasis
choosing people by their skills and test results

look.title: Who Counts in the Census
look.prompt: About what share of India's people belonged to Scheduled Castes or Scheduled Tribes combined in 2011?

check.q: What are reservations in India?
choices: Seats set aside for groups held back by caste
check.why: Reservations set aside seats in colleges, jobs and legislatures for groups held back by caste.

check.q: Who are Scheduled Tribes?
check.why: Scheduled Tribes are Indigenous communities, often called Adivasis.

check.q: What is one criticism of reservations named in the lesson?
choices: They are too new to judge
Seats should go by merit or income, not group
check.why: Critics argue for merit or family income, and say the better-off in each group gain most.

lessons.title: Change, Hope and Unfinished Work
lessons.mainIdea: Caste has weakened in many areas of life, but it still shapes marriage, work and politics for many.
reading: In 1997 K. R. Narayanan became President of India. He was born into a Dalit family in Kerala, in a thatched hut. He was the first Dalit to hold the country's highest office. His life shows how much can change within one lifetime.

In big cities, people of different jatis ride the same trains, study together and work side by side. Many young people choose their own partners. Yet surveys find most marriages in India still happen inside the same caste. Laws such as a 1989 act punish attacks on Dalits and Adivasis, because such attacks still happen.

Indians disagree about the way forward. Some want caste counted in every census so help can be aimed well. Others fear counting keeps caste alive. Some say rising incomes will end it; others say only laws and movements will. Caste is a question inside India, never a verdict on Hindus or any faith.

words.d: treating people unfairly because of the group they belong to
an official count of a country's people

look.title: Religions in India
look.prompt: Caste-like divisions appear in more than one of these faiths. Why does that suggest caste is about social custom as well as religion?

check.q: Why was K. R. Narayanan's presidency important?
choices: He was the first Dalit President of India
check.why: In 1997 Narayanan became the first Dalit to hold India's highest office.

check.q: What do surveys find about marriage in India today?
choices: Marriage across caste is required by law
Most marriages still happen inside the same caste
check.why: Surveys find most marriages in India still take place within the same caste.

check.q: What is one debate the lesson describes?
choices: Whether caste should be counted in the census
check.why: Some want caste counted so help can be aimed well; others fear counting keeps caste alive.

choices: Varna: thousands of local groups; jati: four groups
Varna: four groups in old texts; jati: local birth groups
Varna: a kitchen; jati: a temple
Varna: a law; jati: a court
review.why: Varna is the four-part idea in texts; jati is the local birth group of daily life.

review.q: Which group did the varna texts link with rulers and warriors?
review.why: Kshatriyas were the rulers and warriors.

review.q: What name did many people once called untouchable choose for themselves?
review.why: Many chose Dalit, meaning broken or crushed, as a name of pride and protest.

review.q: Which religious practice shows equality by having everyone eat together?
review.why: At the langar people of every background sit and eat the same food.

review.q: What did Ambedkar and Gandhi disagree about in 1932?
review.why: They both opposed untouchability but disagreed about separate elections, settled by the Poona Pact.

review.q: Which article of India's Constitution abolishes untouchability?
A student reads: 'Seats should go by family income, not group.' Whose view is this?
review.why: Critics of reservations argue for income or merit instead of group.

review.q: Why did Ambedkar and many followers become Buddhists in 1956?
choices: He wanted a faith built on equality and reason
review.why: Ambedkar said he wanted a faith built on equality and reason.

chapters.title: China and Japan: Scholars and Samurai
chapters.bigQuestion: What happens when a society's official ranking of people no longer matches who holds wealth and power?

story.title: The Bow on the Bridge
story.kicker: A rich merchant in old Edo steps aside for a poor samurai, because the law says rank matters more than money.
paragraphs: Picture a spring morning in Edo, the city we now call Tokyo, around the year 1750. A cloth merchant we will call Kichibei walks across a wooden bridge. His shop is one of the busiest in the city. Lords borrow money from men like him. He eats well and lives in a large house behind his shop.

Coming the other way is a samurai. His robe is faded and patched. His rice stipend, the yearly pay his lord gives him, has not risen in years, and he owes money to shopkeepers. But two swords hang at his waist. Only samurai were allowed to wear two swords in public.

Kichibei stops, steps to the side of the bridge and bows low. The samurai walks past without a word. Kichibei knows the rules. Under the Tokugawa government, samurai stood at the top of the official order. Merchants stood at the bottom of the four ranks, no matter how rich they were. A merchant who was rude to a samurai could be punished severely.

Yet by evening, the same samurai may visit Kichibei's shop to ask for more time on a debt. This was the puzzle of Tokugawa Japan. The official ranking said one thing. Money often said another. Over time, that gap helped push Japan toward great change.
story.think: Who really had more power on that bridge, the merchant or the samurai? What kinds of power can a person have?

lessons.title: Four Kinds of People
lessons.mainIdea: Chinese thinkers ranked society as scholars, farmers, artisans and merchants.
reading: Confucius was a teacher who lived in China about 2,500 years ago. He taught that society works best when people know their roles and act with respect. Rulers should be wise and caring. Children should honor parents. Later thinkers who followed his ideas are called Confucians.

Confucian writers described four kinds of people. At the top were *scholars*, educated men who served in government. Next came farmers, who grew the food everyone needed. Then artisans, who made tools and goods. Last came merchants, who bought and sold. Many writers called merchants less useful because they did not produce things themselves.

This ranking was an ideal, not a set of castes. People were not locked in by birth. In real life, many merchants grew very rich. Some married their children into scholar families or bought land. The ranking still mattered, because it told people what kind of life earned honor.

words.d: a set of ideas from the teacher Confucius about respect, duty, learning and good government
a highly educated person; in imperial China, one who studied the classics and could serve in government
a person who earns a living by buying and selling goods

look.title: A Ladder of Honor
look.text: Four people stand on a ladder. On the top rung is a scholar with a book. Below him is a farmer with a hoe. Below the farmer is a potter at his wheel. On the bottom rung is a merchant holding a bag of silver, the heaviest bag on the ladder.
look.prompt: Why might Confucian thinkers place the farmer above the merchant, even though the merchant has more money?

check.q: Which group was at the top of the Confucian ideal order?
check.why: Scholars, educated men who served in government, were placed at the top.

lessons.title: The Great Examinations
lessons.mainIdea: China chose many officials through hard written exams, a path upward that lasted until 1905.
reading: Imagine a young man in a small, bare cell, one of thousands in a long row. He has brought food, ink, brushes and a blanket. For days he will write essays on ancient books he has memorized since boyhood. Guards patrol outside. If he passes, his whole family's life may change.

This was the *civil-service examination*. A civil service is the group of officials who run a government. China began using written exams to choose officials about 1,400 years ago. The system grew much larger under the Song dynasty, about a thousand years ago. Tests covered the Confucian classics, poetry and questions of government.

The exams came in levels, from local to provincial to a final exam in the capital. The top degree was called *jinshi*. Only a tiny share of candidates passed the highest levels. The system lasted until the Qing government ended it in 1905, as China sought modern schools.

words.d: a written test used in imperial China to choose government officials
the highest degree in China's examination system
a family that rules a country for many generations

look.title: The Exam System Over Time
look.cite: Benjamin A. Elman, A Cultural History of Civil Examinations in Late Imperial China, 2000
look.prompt: About how many years did China use civil-service exams in some form?

check.q: What is a civil service?
choices: The group of officials who run a government
check.why: A civil service is the body of officials who run a government.

check.q: What did the exams mostly test?
choices: The Confucian classics, poetry and government
check.why: Candidates wrote essays on the Confucian classics, poetry and government questions.

check.q: When did the Qing government end the exams?
check.why: The exams ended in 1905 as China moved toward modern schools.

lessons.title: A Ladder That Was Hard to Climb
lessons.mainIdea: The exams opened a path up in theory, but wealth made it much easier to climb.
reading: In principle, most men could sit for the exams, whatever their family's rank. A farmer's son who studied hard might become a high official. Stories of such success were told and retold. Supporters of the system praised it as a way to reward talent instead of noble birth.

In practice, preparing took many years of study. A family needed money to hire tutors and to spare a son from farm work. So most successful candidates came from families that already had land or learning. Some villages and family groups pooled money to support one bright boy, hoping his success would lift them all.

The exams also shaped who held power in local life. Men who passed even the lower levels joined the *gentry*, a respected class of educated landowners. Women could not take the exams at all. Historians still debate how much the system truly allowed *social mobility*, meaning movement up or down in rank.

words.d: in imperial China, a respected local class of educated landowners, many with exam degrees
the ability of people to move up or down in wealth or rank
a natural ability or skill that can be developed

look.title: Two Boys, One Exam
look.text: Boy A's father owns land and a library. A tutor teaches him every day from age six. Boy B's father rents a small field. Boy B studies at night by a weak lamp after helping in the field. Both are equally bright. Both take the same exam at age twenty.
look.prompt: The exam is the same for both. Is the contest fair? Give one reason for yes and one for no.

check.q: Why did most successful candidates come from wealthy families?
choices: Preparing took years and cost money for tutors
The tests were in a foreign language
check.why: Years of study and tutors cost money that poorer families rarely had.

check.q: What does social mobility mean?
choices: Moving up or down in wealth or rank
check.why: Social mobility is movement up or down in wealth or rank.

check.q: Who could not take China's civil-service exams?
check.why: Women were not allowed to sit for the exams.

lessons.title: Peace and Order After War
lessons.mainIdea: The Tokugawa shoguns ended a long age of war and ruled Japan from about 1603 to 1868.
reading: For more than a hundred years before 1600, Japan was torn by wars between local lords. Then three strong leaders united the country. The last of them, Tokugawa Ieyasu, won a great battle at Sekigahara in 1600. In 1603 he took the title *shogun*, the top military ruler.

Japan still had an emperor in Kyoto, honored as the country's ancient ruler. But the shogun held real power from his city of Edo. The Tokugawa family kept that power for about 265 years. This time is called the Tokugawa or Edo period. It was a long age of peace inside Japan.

The shoguns kept peace partly through strict order. Regional lords, called *daimyo*, had to spend every other year in Edo. Their families stayed there as a guarantee. This rule, called alternate attendance, kept lords loyal and busy. It also cost them great sums on travel.

words.d: the top military ruler of Japan, who held real power while the emperor reigned in name
a regional lord in Japan who ruled land and commanded samurai
the Tokugawa rule that lords live in Edo every other year

look.title: A Lord on the Road
look.text: A long procession winds along a highway. Hundreds of samurai, porters and servants carry chests, banners and a covered chair for their lord. They are traveling to Edo, a trip of many days. The lord must pay for every inn, every meal and every horse.
look.prompt: How might this costly trip, made again and again, help the shogun keep control over the lords?

check.why: Tokugawa Ieyasu took the title shogun in 1603.

check.why: Daimyo were regional lords who ruled land and commanded samurai.

lessons.title: Samurai, Farmers, Artisans, Merchants
lessons.mainIdea: Tokugawa Japan used a four-rank order with samurai on top and merchants at the bottom.
reading: The Tokugawa borrowed the old Chinese list of four kinds of people. But in Japan, the top rank was not scholars. It was the *samurai*, the warrior class. Samurai made up a small share of the people, often estimated at about 6 percent. Below them came farmers, then artisans, then merchants.

In the long peace, few samurai ever fought a battle. Many worked as officials, clerks and teachers for their lords. They were paid a yearly *stipend* in rice. They had special rights, such as wearing two swords and having family names. A person was born into samurai rank and usually could not leave it.

Below the four ranks were outcast groups, whose jobs, such as leather work, were seen as unclean. They faced harsh separation. Their descendants, known as Burakumin, later organized to fight discrimination, starting in the 1920s. The four-rank order was never a full picture of Japanese life, but it set the rules.

words.d: the hereditary warrior class of Japan, ranked at the top of the Tokugawa order
a fixed regular payment; samurai stipends were paid in rice
passed down from parents to children

look.title: Same List, Different Top
look.text: China's ideal order: scholars, farmers, artisans, merchants. Tokugawa Japan's order: samurai, farmers, artisans, merchants. In China, a man could reach the top by passing exams. In Japan, a man reached the top by being born into a samurai family.
look.prompt: What does the change at the top of the list tell you about what each society honored most?

check.q: Which group was at the top of the Tokugawa order?
check.why: In Japan the samurai, the warrior class, stood at the top.

check.q: How were most samurai paid during the Tokugawa peace?
check.why: Samurai received a yearly stipend paid in rice.

check.q: How did a person usually become a samurai?
choices: By being born into a samurai family
check.why: Samurai rank was hereditary, passed from parents to children.

lessons.title: When Money Outgrew Rank
lessons.mainIdea: Merchants grew rich in Tokugawa cities while many samurai fell into debt.
reading: Peace brought roads, markets and cities. Edo grew into one of the largest cities in the world, with many hundreds of thousands of people. Scholars' estimates for the 1700s run from about 700,000 to a million. Osaka became a great center of rice trading. Merchants handled that rice, lent money and ran large shops. The Mitsui family opened a famous cloth store in Edo in 1673.

Samurai stipends were fixed in rice, but prices and costs kept changing. Many samurai families borrowed from merchants to keep up with their duties. Lords borrowed too. A merchant could hold more wealth than a samurai while still ranking below him.

The government tried *sumptuary laws*, rules limiting what each rank could wear or spend. Merchants were told not to wear silk in public, for example. Many found quiet ways around these rules. City culture, with kabuki theater and colorful woodblock prints, grew from merchant money and tastes.

words.d: rules that limit what people of each rank may wear, own or spend
money that a person owes to someone else

look.title: Great Cities Around 1800
look.cite: Tertius Chandler, Four Thousand Years of Urban Growth, 1987
look.prompt: Edo was among the world's largest cities. Why would a big city give merchants more chances than a village?

check.q: Why did many samurai fall into debt?
choices: Their stipends were fixed while costs changed
They were not allowed to eat rice
Merchants refused to trade with them
They paid high taxes to farmers
check.why: Fixed rice stipends could not keep up with changing prices and costs.

check.q: What were sumptuary laws?
choices: Rules limiting what each rank could wear or spend
check.why: Sumptuary laws set limits on dress and spending by rank.

check.q: Which art forms grew from merchant money and tastes?
check.why: Kabuki and colorful woodblock prints grew from city merchant culture.

lessons.title: A New Government in 1868
lessons.mainIdea: In 1868 reformers restored the emperor's rule and began to rebuild Japan quickly.
reading: In 1853 American warships under Commodore Matthew Perry sailed into Edo Bay. They demanded that Japan open its ports to trade. The shogun's government gave in. Many Japanese feared their country would be taken over by Western powers, as parts of China had been.

Young samurai from southwestern domains, such as Satsuma and Choshu, turned against the shogun. In 1868 they took power in the name of the young Emperor Meiji. This event is called the *Meiji Restoration*. Restoration means bringing back; they said they were bringing back the emperor's rule.

The new leaders moved fast to *modernize*, to build railways, factories, schools and a modern army and navy. They sent students abroad to learn Western science and law. The capital moved to Edo, renamed Tokyo, meaning eastern capital.

words.d: the 1868 change that ended the shogun's rule and put the emperor at the center of a new government
to change a country with new technology, schools and ways of governing

look.title: The Charter Oath
look.text: The new government promised that decisions would be made after wide discussion, that all classes would work together, that common people could follow their own callings, and that knowledge would be sought throughout the world.
look.cite: The Charter Oath, issued in the name of Emperor Meiji, 1868
look.prompt: Which promise in the oath would matter most to a merchant or a farmer? Why?

check.q: What happened in 1853 that alarmed many Japanese?
choices: American warships under Perry demanded open ports
check.why: Perry's warships arrived in 1853 and demanded that Japan open to trade.

check.q: What does restoration mean in Meiji Restoration?
check.why: Restoration means bringing back; leaders said they were restoring the emperor's rule.

check.q: What new name was given to Edo?
check.why: Edo was renamed Tokyo, meaning eastern capital.

lessons.title: The End of the Samurai Class
lessons.mainIdea: Meiji reforms abolished samurai privileges and made all men equal subjects under one law.
reading: The Meiji leaders were mostly samurai themselves. Yet they decided their own class had to go. In 1871 they abolished the lords' domains and made them prefectures run by Tokyo. They declared the four ranks legally equal and ended the separate status of outcast groups, at least on paper.

In 1873 a new law called for *conscription*, drafting young men of every class into a national army. Farmers' sons now carried rifles, a job once reserved for samurai. In 1876 samurai lost their stipends, turned into government bonds, and were banned from wearing swords in public.

Some samurai rebelled. In 1877 Saigo Takamori led the Satsuma Rebellion, the last great samurai uprising. The new army of commoners defeated it. Former samurai found new work as officers, teachers, officials and business owners. Some fell into poverty. A new ranking of nobles and commoners replaced the old one.

words.d: a law that requires people to serve in the military
a special right held only by some people
an armed fight against a government

look.prompt: How many years passed between the Restoration and the last great samurai rebellion?

check.q: What happened in 1876?
choices: Samurai stipends ended and swords were banned in public
check.why: In 1876 stipends were turned into bonds and wearing swords in public was banned.

check.q: Who led the Satsuma Rebellion in 1877?
check.why: Saigo Takamori led the last great samurai uprising.

lessons.title: Korea's Yangban
lessons.mainIdea: In Joseon Korea, the yangban elite gained office through exams, while other classes stood below them.
reading: The Joseon dynasty ruled Korea from 1392 until the early 1900s. Like China, Joseon honored Confucian learning and chose officials through exams called *gwageo*. The families who held office and land were called *yangban*. The name means two groups, for the civil and military officials who stood on two sides of the king.

Below the yangban were several groups. Chungin were skilled specialists, such as interpreters and doctors. Most people were commoners who farmed. At the bottom were the *cheonmin*, the lowborn, including many enslaved people and some workers in low-ranked jobs. Birth mattered a great deal in Joseon.

Joseon also shows that rank could be questioned from the top. King Sejong's scholars created Hangul, a simple Korean alphabet, in the 1440s so that ordinary people could read. In 1894 the Gabo Reforms officially ended class distinctions and slavery in Korea.

words.d: the educated, land-holding elite of Joseon Korea, from whom most officials came
Korea's civil-service examinations
the lowborn class of Joseon Korea, including many enslaved people

look.title: Letters for Everyone
look.text: The king writes that ordinary people often have things they wish to say but cannot write them down. Feeling sorry for them, he has made a small set of new letters, easy to learn and use every day.
look.cite: King Sejong, preface to Hunminjeongeum (The Correct Sounds for Teaching the People), 1446
look.prompt: How might an easy alphabet change the power of the yangban, who could read difficult Chinese characters?

check.q: Who were the yangban?
check.why: The yangban were the elite families who held land and office in Joseon Korea.

check.q: What was the gwageo?
check.why: Gwageo were the exams Joseon used to choose officials.

check.q: What did the Gabo Reforms of 1894 do?
choices: Officially ended class distinctions and slavery
check.why: The Gabo Reforms ended class distinctions and slavery in law.

lessons.title: How Rank Shaped Daily Life
lessons.mainIdea: Rank showed in clothing, speech, homes and manners across East Asia.
reading: In a Joseon town, you could often tell a yangban man at a glance. He might wear a tall black hat made of horsehair and a flowing white robe. He would not carry heavy loads himself. In Tokugawa Japan, a samurai's two swords and hairstyle showed his rank. Clothing was a public badge.

Speech showed rank too. Korean and Japanese both have *honorifics*, special word forms that show respect to someone of higher rank or age. A commoner spoke to a yangban or samurai with humble words. People bowed lower to those above them. These habits of respect remain part of both languages today, though now they mostly follow age and role.

Rank shaped homes, marriages and even where people could live. Yet people pushed back. Merchants bought fine goods quietly. Farmers sometimes protested unfair taxes in large groups. Rank was powerful, but people were never simply their rank.

words.d: special word forms that show respect to someone of higher rank or age
a person's position or rank in a society
